internal-client-error.plainTitle: Pages or files that can't be found
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site answer with an error instead of a page or file, most often "not found" (a 404).
Visitors who follow a link to one get an error page, and Google drops addresses like these from its results.
That's the right answer for something you removed on purpose, as long as nothing still links to it.
plainFix: Look at each address in the list and decide whether it should still exist.
If it should, put the page or file back.
If it has moved, forward the old address to the new one (a "301 redirect"), in your site's redirect settings or through your developer.
If it's gone for good, leave it, and remove the links that still point to it.
internal-client-error.plainPassed: No page or file answers with a "not found" error

internal-server-error.plainTitle: Pages or files that fail with a server error
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site answer with a server error, such as "internal server error" (a 500).
Visitors see an error page, and Google visits a site less often while the errors go on.
One error on a busy day can be a blip, but errors that repeat mean something on the server is broken.
plainFix: Open two or three of the addresses in your browser to see whether they still fail.
If they do, send the list to your developer or hosting company: the cause will be in the server's error log.
If they load now, check the site again at the "Polite" speed: the check itself may have been too much for the server.
internal-server-error.plainPassed: No page or file fails with a server error

internal-unreachable.plainTitle: Pages or files that don't answer
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site gave no answer at all: the connection failed, or the wait ran out.
Visitors get a browser error or a page that never loads, and Google can't list an address it gets nothing from.
It can also happen when the check itself asks faster than the server can cope with.
plainFix: Open two or three of the addresses in your browser to see whether they load for you.
If they don't, send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask what is dropping or delaying connections.
If they do, check the site again at the "Polite" speed to see whether the check was too much for the server.
internal-unreachable.plainPassed: No page or file failed to answer

internal-blocked.plainTitle: Pages or files that refused the check
plainWhat: Your site's firewall or security service turned the check away from some addresses, so they couldn't be read.
Any problems on those addresses are missing from these results.
Visitors rarely notice, but if search engines are turned away too, they can't list those addresses.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser to see that it loads for you.
Ask your hosting company, or whoever runs the firewall, to let Shouting Iguana through, then check the site again.
Ask them to make sure Google and other search engines aren't turned away by the same rules.
internal-blocked.plainPassed: No page or file refused the check

content-type-mismatch.plainTitle: Files your server labels as the wrong kind
plainWhat: Your pages use these files as code, a style sheet or a picture, but your server says they're something else.
Browsers often refuse to use code or a style sheet labelled wrongly, so the page can break for visitors and for Google.
A "picture" that turns out to be a web page is usually an error page in disguise.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it says how each file is used and what the server calls it.
Ask them to set the server to label each kind of file correctly, or to fix the address that loads it.
content-type-mismatch.plainPassed: Every file is labelled as the right kind

soft-404.plainTitle: Pages that read like an error page
plainWhat: These pages have a title or main heading that reads like an error message, such as "Page not found", and little text.
Yet they tell search engines they loaded normally, so Google keeps coming back to pages it won't show (it calls them "soft 404s").
If a page is real and its heading only mentions "not found", there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open each page in the list and see whether it's a real page or an error message.
If it's a real page, change the title or heading so it doesn't read like an error.
If it's an error message, ask your developer to make the address answer "not found" (a 404), or forward it to a replacement.
soft-404.plainPassed: No page reads like an error page

redirect-chain.plainTitle: Addresses that forward more than once
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site forward visitors on two or more times before they reach the final address.
Each extra step is a wait before the page starts to load, and Google gives up after 10 steps.
Two steps do little harm, but the steps pile up each time the site changes.
plainFix: Change the links on your pages, and the addresses in your sitemap, to the final address: the list shows it.
Ask your developer or hosting company to forward each old address straight to the final one, in one step (a "301 redirect").
redirect-chain.plainPassed: No address forwards more than once

redirect-loop.plainTitle: Addresses that forward in a circle
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site forward visitors round in a circle, so they never reach a page.
The browser gives up and shows an error such as "too many redirects", and search engines have nothing to list.
The usual cause is two forwarding rules that undo each other, such as one adding a slash to an address and one removing it.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser to see the error for yourself.
Send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask them to find the two forwarding rules that undo each other.
Ask them to make each address end at a page that loads, then check the site again.
redirect-loop.plainPassed: No address forwards in a circle

redirect-broken.plainTitle: Addresses that forward to a dead end
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site forward visitors on, but to an address that doesn't work, or to nowhere at all.
Visitors land on an error instead of the page they were promised, and search engines find nothing to list.
Every link to the old address, on your site and on others, leads to that error.
plainFix: Look at where each address in the list ends up, and decide which working page should replace it.
Change the forwarding (the "redirect") to point at that page, in your site's redirect settings or through your developer.
If nothing replaces it, remove the forwarding so the old address answers "not found" (a 404), then remove the links to it.
redirect-broken.plainPassed: No address forwards to a dead end

plainWhat: Some addresses forward visitors to another of your pages with a signal that the move is only temporary.
Google may then keep the old address in its results, which delays the switch when the move is really for good.
That's right for a short-term move, such as a sale page, and then there's nothing to do.
Forwarding to another website, such as a hosted checkout, isn't listed.
plainFix: Look at each address in the list and decide whether its move is for good.
If it's temporary, leave it.
If it's for good, ask your developer or hosting company to change it from temporary (a "302 redirect") to permanent (a "301 redirect").
redirect-temporary.plainPassed: No forwarding is marked as temporary

redirect-temporary-cached.plainTitle: Temporary forwarding that browsers remember for days
plainWhat: These addresses forward visitors with a temporary move, but tell browsers they may remember it for more than a day.
Visitors' browsers may keep sending them to the old place for days after you change it.
plainFix: If the move is for good, ask your developer to make it permanent (a "301 redirect").
If it's temporary, ask for it to be sent with an instruction not to remember it ("Cache-Control: no-store").
redirect-temporary-cached.plainPassed: No temporary forwarding is remembered for days

redirect-downgrade.plainTitle: Secure addresses that forward to an insecure one
plainWhat: Some secure addresses on your site (starting "https") forward visitors to an insecure one (starting "http").
Browsers label the page they land on "Not secure", and Google is then likely to list the insecure address.
The usual cause is an old forwarding rule that was never updated.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser and look for "Not secure" beside the address it ends on.
Send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask them to forward each one to the "https" version of where it goes.
Check the site again once it's changed.
redirect-downgrade.plainPassed: No secure address forwards to an insecure one

meta-refresh.plainTitle: Pages that move on or reload by themselves
plainWhat: These pages send visitors to another address, or reload, by themselves: at once, or after a set time.
A timed move takes the page away while people are still reading.
It's also slower than forwarding done by the server, which is what Google recommends.
It's an acceptable fallback only where the server can't forward.
plainFix: Open one of the pages and watch what happens: the list shows where each one sends visitors, and when.
Ask your developer to replace it (it's called a "meta refresh") with forwarding done by the server (a "301 redirect").
If a page reloads to show fresh content, ask for it to update in place instead, or leave visitors to reload.
meta-refresh.plainPassed: No page moves on or reloads by itself
meta-refresh.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one line in your page design, which every page shares.

broken-internal-links.plainTitle: Links that lead to broken pages
plainWhat: Some of your pages have links that lead to an address on your site that doesn't work.
Visitors who click one land on an error page, and search engines waste their visit on it.
A link in a menu or footer repeats on every page, so one bad link can show up hundreds of times.
plainFix: Open each page in the list in your site's editor and find the link.
Point it at the right page, or remove it.
If the same link is on most pages, it's in your menu, footer or page design: fix it there once.
broken-internal-links.plainPassed: Every link between your pages leads to a working page

broken-external-links.plainTitle: Links to other websites that don't work
plainWhat: Some of your pages link to an address on another website that doesn't work.
Visitors who click one reach a dead end, which makes your page look out of date.
Some websites turn away automatic checks but work for people, so try a link yourself before you change it.
Links that another website's security or rules file kept the check from opening aren't counted.
plainFix: Click a few of the links in your browser to confirm they're really broken.
Open each page in your site's editor and point the link at the new address, if the page has moved.
Remove the link, or swap it for another source, if the page has gone for good.
broken-external-links.plainPassed: No link to another website was found broken
broken-external-links.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your menu, footer or page design, which every page shares.

links-to-redirects.plainTitle: Links that go through a forwarding address
plainWhat: Some links on your pages point at an address on your site that forwards visitors on for good.
The link still works, but each click takes an extra step, as does each search engine visit.
A few do no harm, so there's nothing to do unless the link is in a menu or footer on every page.
Forwarding that's only for now, such as a sign-in link's, isn't listed.
plainFix: Open a page from the list in your site's editor and find the link: the list shows the address it points at.
Change the link to the address it ends up at.
Leave the forwarding itself in place, for bookmarks and for links from other websites.
links-to-redirects.plainPassed: No link between your pages goes through a forwarding address
links-to-redirects.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your menu, footer or page design, which every page shares.

internal-nofollow-links.plainTitle: Links that search engines are told not to follow
plainWhat: Some links between your own pages carry a note that tells search engines not to follow them.
Pages reached only through links like these (marked "nofollow") may be found late by search engines, or not at all.
It's common on login and basket links, where it does little harm and little good.
plainFix: Open a page from the list in your site's editor and find the link: the list shows where it leads.
Remove the "nofollow" setting from the link, often a tick box in the link's options.
If the link is in your menu, footer or page design, ask your developer to take the setting off there, once.
If the aim was to keep a page out of search results, ask your developer to set that on the page itself (a "noindex" setting).
internal-nofollow-links.plainPassed: No link between your pages is marked not to be followed
internal-nofollow-links.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your menu, footer or page design, which every page shares.

plainWhat: Some links on your pages have no words: usually an image or icon, such as a logo, with no description.
People who use a screen reader hear only "link", and search engines learn nothing about the page it leads to.
A logo or icon in the page design is the usual cause, so one fix often clears every page.
Pages are still found either way, so it can wait.
plainFix: Find the link on one of the pages: the list shows where it leads.
If it's an image, give the image a short description (its "alt text"), such as your site's name for a logo.
If it's an icon, ask your developer to add a label to the link (an "aria-label").
empty-anchor-text.plainPassed: Every link between your pages has words to read
empty-anchor-text.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly your logo, which sits in the part of the site every page shares.

broken-fragment-links.plainTitle: Links to a part of a page that isn't there
plainWhat: Some links point to a part of a page, such as a heading further down, but that part can't be found.
Visitors land at the top of the page instead of the section the link promised.
Search engines still follow the link to the page, so only visitors are affected.
Some pages build their sections after loading, so if a link works in your browser there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Click the link on one of the pages and see whether it jumps to the right section.
If it doesn't, compare the part of the link after the "#" with the name the section was given (its "anchor" or "id").
Make the two match exactly in your site's editor, or ask your developer to put the name back on the section.
broken-fragment-links.plainPassed: No link points to a missing part of a page
broken-fragment-links.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your page design, such as "Skip to content", which every page shares.

orphan-page.plainTitle: Pages in your sitemap that nothing links to
plainWhat: No page on your site links to these pages, or only with links search engines are told not to follow.
Visitors can't reach them by browsing, and Google relies on links to find pages and judge what they're about.
They're often old pages left in the sitemap (the file that lists your pages for search engines), or pages reached only through a form.
plainFix: Decide, for each page, whether you still want it.
If you do, link to it from a page where it belongs, such as its category.
If you don't, remove it from the site and from the sitemap.
orphan-page.plainPassed: No page in the sitemap is left with no links to it

plainWhat: Some links on these pages work only through code in the browser, so search engines can't follow them.
Pages reached only through such links may never be found in search.
Menus and "load more" buttons are the usual cause.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the first few such links on each page, and what's wrong with each.
Ask for each one to be a normal link with a real web address, with any code kept on top of it.
uncrawlable-links.plainPassed: Every link can be followed by search engines
uncrawlable-links.plainOneFix: If most pages are listed, it's almost certainly your menu, which every page shares.

broken-resources.plainTitle: Pages that load files that are missing
plainWhat: These pages load a file, such as code, a style sheet or a video, that is missing or fails.
The page can look or work wrong for visitors, and for Google, which loads pages as visitors do.
A broken file from another company's service often changes nothing anyone sees.
plainFix: Open one of the pages and check that it looks and works as it should.
Send the list to your developer: each page names the missing file.
Ask them to restore each file, correct its address, or remove what's no longer used.
broken-resources.plainPassed: No page loads a file that is missing

links-to-localhost.plainTitle: Links to a test copy that only works for whoever built it
plainWhat: These pages link to an address that exists only on someone's own computer or private network, such as "localhost".
Everyone else gets a dead link, or a missing picture or file.
It's usually left behind when content was copied over from a test copy of the site.
plainFix: Open each page and find the link: the list shows the first such address on each.
Change it to the address on your live site, or remove it.
links-to-localhost.plainPassed: No page links to a test copy of the site

few-internal-outlinks.plainTitle: Dead-end pages that link to nothing else on your site
plainWhat: These pages have fewer than {limit:minInternalOutlinks} to other pages of your site.
Visitors who land on one have nowhere obvious to go next, and search engines find no way onward from it.
It's common on pages built without your site's usual menu and footer.
plainFix: Add links from each page to related pages and to its section.
If a page is missing your site's menu and footer, use your normal page design for it.
few-internal-outlinks.plainPassed: Every page links on to other pages of the site

generic-anchor-text.plainTitle: Links that say "click here" instead of where they go
plainWhat: Some links on these pages say only "click here", "read more" or the like, not where they lead.
People using screen readers often hear a page's links on their own, where those words mean nothing.
Google also uses a link's words to understand the page it leads to.
plainFix: Change each link's words to say what's at the other end, such as "Read our delivery policy".
The list shows the words each page uses.
generic-anchor-text.plainPassed: No link says only "click here" or the like

non-indexable-inlinks-only.plainTitle: Pages only linked from pages Google won't show
plainWhat: The only pages that link to these are themselves kept out of search results, or point Google at another page.
Search engines can still reach them, but such links count for little.
It's often a page linked only from filtered lists, or from page 2 of a list that points Google at page 1.
plainFix: Keep the links you have: they're how search engines reach these pages.
If page 2 of a list links here but points Google at page 1, ask your developer to let each page stand for itself.
If they're kept out on purpose, like filtered lists, link to each page from one that appears in search, such as its category.
non-indexable-inlinks-only.plainPassed: Every page has a link from a page Google can show

deep-page.plainTitle: Pages buried deep in your site
plainWhat: These pages are more than {limit:maxClickDepth} away from your home page.
Search engines tend to visit deep pages less often, and visitors rarely click that far.
Big shops have some deep pages by design, so look at which pages these are.
plainFix: Link to the pages that matter from higher up, such as a category page, the menu or the home page.
Add subcategories, so long lists don't push pages further down.
deep-page.plainPassed: No page is buried deep in the site

plainWhat: These pages have more than {limit:maxInternalLinks} to your own pages, or more than {limit:maxExternalLinks} to other websites.
So many links are hard for visitors to use, and each one counts for less.
It's usually a huge menu or footer.
plainFix: Cut the links down to the ones visitors use, starting with the menu and footer.
Split very long lists over several pages.
too-many-links.plainPassed: No page is crowded with links

slow-external-links.plainTitle: Links to other websites that take a long time to load
plainWhat: These pages link to pages on other websites that took more than {limit:slowExternalLinkMs} to answer.
Visitors who follow the link wait, and may blame your site.
Another website being slow once can be a blip, so check before changing anything.
plainFix: Open the slowest links to see whether they're slow for you too.
Replace a link that stays slow with a better source, or remove it.
slow-external-links.plainPassed: No link leads to a slow page on another website

pagination-not-linked.plainTitle: Next pages of a list that only hidden links point to
plainWhat: These pages of a list point to the next or previous page only through hidden links in the page's code.
Google no longer reads those, and finds the other pages of a list only through ordinary links.
Pages reached only that way may never be found.
plainFix: Ask your developer to add ordinary "Next" and "Previous" links, or page numbers, between the pages of each list.
pagination-not-linked.plainPassed: Every page of a list links to the next with a normal link

pagination-broken.plainTitle: Next or previous page links that lead to an error
plainWhat: The hidden links these pages use to name the next or previous page of a list lead to an error, or forward elsewhere.
It usually means the list's addresses changed and the page design didn't follow.
plainFix: Ask your developer to point the hidden "next" and "prev" links at the right pages, or remove them.
pagination-broken.plainPassed: No next or previous page link leads to an error

pagination-to-non-indexable.plainTitle: Next or previous page links to pages Google won't show
plainWhat: The hidden links these pages use to name the next or previous page of a list lead to a page kept out of search.
What's listed only on that page is then found only through a page search engines drop.
plainFix: Ask your developer whether the list's pages should appear in search.
If they should, have the setting that keeps them out removed; if not, have the links point at pages that do appear.
pagination-to-non-indexable.plainPassed: No next or previous page link leads to a hidden page

pagination-sequence-error.plainTitle: Next and previous page links that don't match up
plainWhat: The hidden links these pages use to name the next and previous page of a list don't make a sequence.
A page names itself as next, names two next pages, or its next page doesn't name it back.
Google no longer reads these links, so it's a tidy-up rather than a search problem.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it says what's wrong on each page.
Ask for each page to name one next and one previous page, in order.
pagination-sequence-error.plainPassed: Every list's next and previous page links match up

noindex-page.plainTitle: Pages told to stay out of search results
plainWhat: These pages carry an instruction that tells search engines to keep them out of search results.
Google drops such a page from its results completely (the instruction is called "noindex").
That's right for thank-you, account and site-search pages, and then there's nothing to do.
It's a problem only on a page you want people to find, where it's often left over from when the site was built.
plainFix: Look down the list for any page you want people to find in search.
Open that page in your site's editor and find a setting such as "Hide this page from search engines", often under "SEO".
Turn the setting off, or ask your developer to remove the "noindex" from the page.
noindex-page.plainPassed: No page is told to stay out of search results

nofollow-page.plainTitle: Pages that tell search engines not to follow their links
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines not to follow any of the links on them.
Pages that are linked only from here may never be found by search engines.
That's rarely meant: it's usually left over from when the site was built, or set by a plugin.
plainFix: Open one of the pages in your site's editor and find a setting about following links, often under "SEO" or "Advanced".
Set it to follow links, or ask your developer to remove the "nofollow" setting from the page.
If only one or two links shouldn't be followed, ask your developer to mark those links instead of the whole page.
nofollow-page.plainPassed: No page tells search engines not to follow its links

blocked-by-robots.plainTitle: Addresses that search engines are told not to visit
plainWhat: Your site's rules file for search engines puts these addresses off limits, so the check didn't read them.
Search engines can't see what's on them, though Google may still list the bare address if other pages link to it.
That's right for baskets and site searches, and then there's nothing to do.
It's a problem if the rule catches pages you want found.
plainFix: Look down the list for any page you want people to find, and for files ending in .css or .js, which pages need to display.
If there are none, leave the rules as they are.
If there are, ask your developer to change the rule that covers them in the rules file (its "robots.txt").
If the list says the rules file couldn't be read, fix that first: it's listed as a problem of its own.
blocked-by-robots.plainPassed: No address is off limits to search engines

snippet-blocked.plainTitle: Pages set to show no text in search results
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines to show no text from the page under its title in search results.
The result is a bare title and address, which tells searchers less, and Google won't quote the page in its AI answers.
That can be deliberate, for private or paid-for content, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Search Google for one of the pages and see whether its result shows any text under the title.
Decide whether you meant these pages to appear that way.
If not, ask your developer to remove the setting the list names, such as "nosnippet", from the pages.
snippet-blocked.plainPassed: No page blocks its text from search results
snippet-blocked.plainOneFix: These pages most likely get it from one setting, in your page design or SEO plugin.

robots-txt-unreachable.plainTitle: Search engines can't read your site's rules file
robots-txt-unreachable.plainLooksFor: A rules file that search engines can't read
plainWhat: The file that tells search engines where they may go on your site (its "robots.txt") answers with an error.
Google stops visiting the whole site when that happens, so new and changed pages don't reach search results.
This is one fault for the whole site, and the first thing to fix.
plainFix: Open your site's address followed by /robots.txt in a browser, to see whether it loads for you.
Send this to your developer or hosting company today: the file must answer normally, or with "not found" if you don't need one.
Ask them to make sure the firewall or security service isn't turning away requests for it.
Check the site again once it's fixed.
robots-txt-unreachable.plainPassed: The rules file for search engines isn't returning an error

robots-txt-unreachable-other-origin.plainTitle: The rules file on another part of your site can't be read
robots-txt-unreachable-other-origin.plainLooksFor: A rules file that fails on another part of your site
plainWhat: The rules file for search engines answers with an error on another part of your site, such as shop.example.com.
Google stops visiting that part of the site when that happens, while your main site carries on as normal.
It matters only if that part holds pages or files you want people to find.
plainFix: Open the address the list names in your browser, to see whether the file loads for you.
Send it to your developer or hosting company: the file (a "robots.txt") must answer normally, or with "not found" if it isn't needed.
If that part of the site shouldn't exist, remove the links to it.
robots-txt-unreachable-other-origin.plainPassed: No other part of the site has a rules file that fails

robots-txt-missing.plainTitle: A rules file for search engines is missing
robots-txt-missing.plainLooksFor: A missing rules file for search engines
plainWhat: Search engines that ask for your site's rules file (a "robots.txt") get "not found", or are refused.
They take that to mean they may visit everything, so nothing is held back.
What you miss is a place to tell them where your sitemap is, and to keep them out of pages such as baskets.
If you need neither, there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the address the list names in a browser, to see what answers.
Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for a "robots.txt" option: most can create the file.
Ask your developer to add one that names your sitemap, if your site has no such option.
Ask your hosting company to let requests for the file through, if a firewall is refusing them.
robots-txt-missing.plainPassed: The site isn't missing its rules file for search engines

site-hidden-from-search.plainTitle: Your site hides most of its pages from search
site-hidden-from-search.plainLooksFor: A site that hides its home page and most pages from search
plainWhat: Your home page and more than half of your pages tell search engines to keep them out of search results.
Those pages can't be found through Google, however good they are.
It's often one setting left on from when the site was being built, so one change may fix it.
This is one fault for the whole site, and the first thing to fix.
plainFix: Look in your site's settings for an option such as "Discourage search engines" or "Hide site from search", and turn it off.
If there's no such option, send this to your developer: the list says how many pages are hidden, and how.
Ask them to remove the "noindex" setting.
Check the site again once it's changed.
site-hidden-from-search.plainPassed: The site as a whole isn't hidden from search

robots-directives-conflict.plainTitle: Pages that tell search engines two different things
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines two opposite things about showing the page in search, or about following its links.
One instruction is in the page itself, and the other is sent by the server along with the page.
Google follows the stricter of the two, so a page meant to appear in search can be left out.
plainFix: Decide which instruction each page should have: the list quotes both.
Ask your developer to make the page and the server say the same thing, or to remove the server's (the "X-Robots-Tag").
robots-directives-conflict.plainPassed: No page tells search engines two different things
robots-directives-conflict.plainOneFix: The same two settings most likely apply to every page listed: one in your page design, one on the server.

noindex-near-home.plainTitle: Important pages kept out of Google
plainWhat: These pages are one or two clicks from your home page, yet they tell search engines to keep them out of search results.
Pages that close to the home page are usually ones you want found, so the instruction ("noindex") is often a leftover.
Basket, account, login and similar pages aren't listed, as they're meant to stay out.
plainFix: Look down the list for any page you want people to find in search.
Open that page in your site's editor and turn off a setting such as "Hide this page from search engines".
If a page is meant to stay out of search, leave it.
noindex-near-home.plainPassed: No page near the home page is kept out of Google

unavailable-after-passed.plainTitle: Pages set to drop out of Google on a date that has passed
plainWhat: These pages tell Google to stop showing them in search after a date, and that date has passed.
Google then drops them from its results, as if they were hidden from search.
The setting is meant for events and offers, and is easily forgotten when a page is kept or reused.
plainFix: Check each page: the list shows the date it gives.
If the page should still appear in search, ask your developer to remove the date setting ("unavailable_after") or move the date on.
If the page really has expired, leave it, or forward it to its replacement.
unavailable-after-passed.plainPassed: No page has passed a date to drop out of Google

media-preview-blocked.plainTitle: Pages that keep their pictures or videos out of Google
plainWhat: These pages tell Google not to show their pictures, or a preview of their videos, in search results.
Their results then stand out less, and the pictures can't be found in image search.
That's often deliberate, for photos you may only use in one place, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Decide whether each page's pictures or videos should appear in Google: the list names the setting each page uses.
If they should, ask your developer to remove that setting, such as "noimageindex" or "max-image-preview:none".
media-preview-blocked.plainPassed: No page keeps its pictures or videos out of Google
media-preview-blocked.plainOneFix: These pages most likely get it from one setting, in your page design or SEO plugin.

translation-blocked.plainTitle: Pages Google won't offer to translate
plainWhat: These pages tell Google not to offer a translation of them to people searching in other languages.
Without that setting, Google can show the result in the searcher's language and link to a translated page.
It's a choice, not a fault: keep it where a machine translation could mislead, such as on legal text.
plainFix: Decide whether people searching in other languages should be offered these pages.
If they should, ask your developer to remove the "notranslate" setting from them.
translation-blocked.plainPassed: No page asks Google not to offer a translation

indexifembedded-without-noindex.plainTitle: Pages with a search setting that does nothing on its own
plainWhat: These pages have a search setting ("indexifembedded") that works only alongside another, which they don't have.
It lets Google show a page's content where another page shows it inside its own, while the page itself stays out of search.
On its own it does nothing, and harms nothing.
plainFix: Ask your developer what the setting was meant to do.
If the pages should appear in search only inside other pages, add the missing "noindex"; otherwise remove "indexifembedded".
indexifembedded-without-noindex.plainPassed: No page has a search setting that does nothing alone

canonicalised-page.plainTitle: Pages that name another page as the main version
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines that another page is the main version of them (a "canonical" link).
Google then shows that other page instead, which is right for true copies, such as a sorted list or a print version.
It's a problem when the page has its own content, as page 2 of a list does: each page of a list should name itself.
plainFix: Look at each page and the page it points to, and decide whether they're really the same thing.
If they are, there's nothing to do.
If this page should appear in search on its own, ask your developer to point its canonical link at its own address.
canonicalised-page.plainPassed: No page names another page as the main version

canonical-missing.plainTitle: Pages that don't name their main address
plainWhat: These pages don't say which address is their main one (they have no "canonical" link).
The same page can often be reached at several addresses, and without this Google picks one itself.
Google usually picks well, so there's nothing to do unless each page can be reached at many addresses.
plainFix: See whether your site's SEO settings or plugin can add a canonical link to every page: most can.
If not, ask your developer to add one to the page design, pointing each page at its own address.
canonical-missing.plainPassed: Every page names its main address

canonical-multiple.plainTitle: Pages that name more than one main address
plainWhat: These pages name two or more different addresses as their main one (they have conflicting "canonical" links).
Google is likely to ignore them all and choose the main address itself.
It usually means two parts of your site each add one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page names a single main address.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a canonical link: it can also come from the server.
canonical-multiple.plainPassed: No page names more than one main address

canonical-broken.plainTitle: Pages that name a broken address as their main one
plainWhat: These pages name a main address that doesn't work (their "canonical" link leads to an error).
Search engines can't show an address that fails, so the instruction does nothing and they choose for themselves.
The cause is usually an out-of-date address, such as one from a test copy of the site.
plainFix: Open the main address the list shows for one of the pages in your browser, to see the error.
If your site's editor has a "canonical" box for the page, often under "SEO", put the page's own address in it.
If the same wrong address is on many pages, ask your developer to correct it in the page design.
canonical-broken.plainPassed: No page names a broken address as its main one
canonical-broken.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

canonical-to-redirect.plainTitle: Pages that name a forwarding address as their main one
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that forwards visitors on to another address.
That gives search engines two answers to one question, and they may not pick the one you want.
Often it forwards straight back to the page itself, which does little harm but is still worth tidying.
plainFix: Look at where each main address in the list ends up: the list names the address, and says when it couldn't be checked.
Put that final address in the "canonical" box of your site's editor, often under "SEO", if it has one.
Ask your developer to correct it in the page design if the same thing shows on many pages.
canonical-to-redirect.plainPassed: No page names a forwarding address as its main one
canonical-to-redirect.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

canonical-to-non-indexable.plainTitle: Pages that name a main address search engines can't show
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that can't itself appear in search results.
The page says "show that one instead", while that one says "don't show me", so the outcome is left to Google.
The list says what holds each one back, such as an instruction to stay out of search.
plainFix: Look at the main address the list shows for each page, and why it can't appear in search.
If that address should appear in search, ask your developer to remove what holds it back.
If it shouldn't, ask them to point the page's canonical link at its own address, or at one that can appear.
canonical-to-non-indexable.plainPassed: No page names a main address that search can't show
canonical-to-non-indexable.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

canonical-outside-head.plainTitle: Main address written in the wrong part of the page
canonical-outside-head.plainLooksFor: Main addresses written in the wrong part of the page
plainWhat: These pages name their main address (a "canonical" link) in a part of the page where search engines ignore it.
So the pages have no main address in effect, and Google chooses one itself.
It usually means something added near the top of the page's code, by a plugin or script, has pushed it out of place.
plainFix: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately, as one of them may be the cause.
Send the list to your developer: the canonical link must sit in the page's "head" section.
Ask them to move or remove whatever ends that section early.
canonical-outside-head.plainPassed: No main address is written in the wrong part of the page

canonical-relative.plainTitle: Main address written as a partial address
canonical-relative.plainLooksFor: Main addresses written as partial addresses
plainWhat: These pages give their main address in a short form, such as /page, without "https://" and your site's name.
Google can read the short form, but recommends the full address.
A short form can end up pointing at the wrong place, for example on a test copy of the site.
If your main addresses already lead to the right pages, there's nothing to do now.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer when they next work on the site: it isn't urgent.
Ask them to write each page's main address (its "canonical" link) in full, starting with "https://" and your site's name.
canonical-relative.plainPassed: No main address is written as a partial address
canonical-relative.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly how your page design or SEO plugin writes the main address on every page.

canonical-invalid.plainTitle: Pages whose main address isn't a real web address
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that is empty or isn't a real web address.
Search engines ignore it, which can leave the page with no main address at all.
It's usually a gap in the page design that was never filled in.
plainFix: Look at what the list shows for each page: it says whether the address is empty or badly formed.
Send the list to your developer and ask them to make each page name its own full address, or remove the broken line.
canonical-invalid.plainPassed: No page names a main address that isn't a real address
canonical-invalid.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a gap in your page design, which writes the same mistake on every page.

noindex-with-canonical.plainTitle: Pages that give search engines two opposite instructions
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines to keep them out of search, and also name another page as their main version.
One instruction says "drop this page", the other says "treat it as a copy of that one", and Google doesn't say which wins.
Each page needs one or the other, not both.
plainFix: Decide, for each page, whether it's a copy of the page it names or a page that should simply stay out of search.
If it's a copy, ask your developer to remove the instruction to stay out of search (the "noindex").
If it should stay out of search, ask them to point its main address (its "canonical" link) at the page itself.
noindex-with-canonical.plainPassed: No page gives search engines opposite instructions
noindex-with-canonical.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

canonical-to-first-page.plainTitle: Later pages of a list that point Google at the first page
plainWhat: These are page 2 onward of a list, such as a category, and each names the list's first page as its main version.
Google may then treat them as copies of the first page and visit them less, so what's listed only further on can go unfound.
Google's advice is for each page of a list to name itself.
plainFix: Ask your developer to make each page of the list name its own address as its main version (its "canonical" link).
Keep the ordinary links between the pages, such as "Next" and the page numbers.
canonical-to-first-page.plainPassed: No later page of a list points Google at the first
canonical-to-first-page.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your shop or SEO plugin, which every list shares.

canonical-other-domain.plainTitle: Pages that tell Google another website has the real copy
plainWhat: These pages name a page on another website as their main version.
Google may then show that website's page instead, and drop yours from its results.
That's right for an article first published elsewhere, but a mistake when it names an old domain or a test copy of your site.
plainFix: Look at the website each page names: the list shows it.
If it's your own old address or a test site, ask your developer to point each page's "canonical" link at its own address.
If the page really is a copy of another website's article, leave it.
canonical-other-domain.plainPassed: No page names another website as its main version

canonical-loop.plainTitle: Pages that point Google at each other in a circle
plainWhat: These pages each name another as their main version, and following those leads back round to where it started.
The instructions cancel out, so Google picks one of the pages itself, which may not be the one you want.
plainFix: Choose which page of each circle should appear in search: the list shows the circle.
Ask your developer to make that page name itself as its main version, and the others name it (their "canonical" links).
canonical-loop.plainPassed: No pages point Google at each other in a circle

canonical-on-redirect.plainTitle: Forwarded addresses that also name a different main address
plainWhat: These addresses forward visitors to another page, and also name a different page as the main version.
Search engines follow the forwarding and ignore the rest, so this changes nothing in search.
It can only mislead people who check the address with a tool, so it isn't urgent.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer when they next work on the site.
Ask them to remove the "canonical" link the server sends with these addresses, or make it name where they lead.
canonical-on-redirect.plainPassed: No forwarded address names a different main address

canonical-fragment.plainTitle: Main addresses with a # part that Google ignores
plainWhat: These pages give their main address with a # part at the end, such as #reviews.
Google ignores everything from the # on, so the main address usually still works.
It's still a mistake, and it can mean the address was copied from the browser rather than set on purpose.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer when they next work on the site: it isn't urgent.
Ask them to remove the # part from each page's main address (its "canonical" link).
canonical-fragment.plainPassed: No main address has a # part
canonical-fragment.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly how your page design or SEO plugin writes the main address on every page.

canonical-invalid-attribute.plainTitle: Main addresses written in a way Google may ignore
plainWhat: These pages name their main address with extra details, such as a language or a screen size, that belong on other links.
Search engines may then not treat it as the page's main address at all.
It's usually a link to a translated or mobile version, written as the main address by mistake.
plainFix: Ask your developer to remove the extra details ("hreflang", "lang", "media" or "type") from each page's "canonical" link.
If the link was meant to point at another version of the page, ask for it to be written as a separate link.
canonical-invalid-attribute.plainPassed: No main address is written in a way Google may ignore

canonical-unlinked.plainTitle: Main versions of pages that nothing links to
plainWhat: Other pages name these pages as their main version, but no page on your site links to them.
Visitors browsing your site only ever reach the other versions, and Google may choose one of those instead.
plainFix: Link to each of these pages wherever its other versions are linked, such as in menus and lists.
If a page shouldn't be the main version, ask your developer to point the others' "canonical" links at one that is linked.
canonical-unlinked.plainPassed: Every main version of a page has links to it

sitemap-non-indexable.plainTitle: Sitemap addresses that can't appear in search
plainWhat: Your sitemap, the file that lists your pages for search engines, includes addresses that can't appear in search.
Each one forwards elsewhere, fails, or is kept out of search some other way: the list says which.
A sitemap should hold only the addresses you want found, and these waste search engines' visits.
plainFix: Look at the reason the list gives for each address.
If the address should be found, fix that reason: it's often listed as a problem of its own.
If it shouldn't, take it out of the sitemap, or list the address it forwards to instead.
Ask your developer to change how the sitemap is built if your site makes it for you and has no setting for this.
sitemap-non-indexable.plainPassed: No sitemap lists an address that can't appear in search

plainWhat: These pages can appear in search, but aren't in your sitemap: the file that lists your pages for search engines.
Search engines can still find them through links, which is enough on a small site.
On a big or fast-changing site, a full sitemap helps new pages get found sooner.
Leaving pages out on purpose is fine, and login, basket and account pages are better kept out of search altogether.
plainFix: Look down the list for pages you want found quickly, such as new products or articles.
Find the sitemap options in your site's SEO settings or plugin, and include the kinds of page that are missing.
Ask your developer to add them if your sitemap is built another way.
not-in-sitemap.plainPassed: No page is missing from the sitemap

sitemap-error.plainTitle: A sitemap on your site can't be read
sitemap-error.plainLooksFor: A sitemap that can't be read
plainWhat: A sitemap your site points search engines to can't be read: it's missing, fails to load, or has mistakes in it.
A sitemap is a file that lists your pages for search engines, and they get nothing from one they can't read.
Pages with links to them are still found, but new pages may take longer to show up in search.
plainFix: Open the sitemap's address from the list in your browser, to see the error.
If your site's SEO settings or plugin make the sitemap, use them to build it again.
If the sitemap no longer exists, ask your developer to remove the line that names it from your rules file (its "robots.txt").
Send the error to your developer otherwise: the file must load and be a valid sitemap of at most 50,000 addresses.
sitemap-error.plainPassed: No sitemap fails to load or has mistakes in it

plainWhat: The check found no sitemap: a file that lists your pages for search engines.
A small site whose pages all link to each other can manage without one, as Google finds pages by following links.
It helps most on big or new sites.
If you gave your sitemap straight to Google, in Search Console, it won't show here, and there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin: most can create a sitemap with one switch.
Ask your developer to add its address to the site's rules file for search engines (its "robots.txt"), so they all find it.
Check the site again: it can then also find pages missing from your sitemap, and pages in it that nothing links to.
sitemap-missing.plainPassed: A sitemap was found, or the site names one

sitemap-url-other-host.plainTitle: Sitemap addresses outside its own website
plainWhat: Your sitemap lists addresses on another website, or on another version of your own, such as with or without "www".
Search engines drop those entries, so the pages they were meant for aren't put forward.
It's common after a site moves to or from "www".
plainFix: Compare the start of the addresses in the list with the start of your sitemap's own address.
Build the sitemap again from your site's SEO settings or plugin, so it lists each page at its current address.
Ask your developer to correct the web address your site is set to, if the sitemap keeps using the old one.
Take out any address that belongs to another website altogether.
sitemap-url-other-host.plainPassed: No sitemap lists an address outside its own website

robots-txt-no-sitemap.plainTitle: Your rules file doesn't say where your sitemap is
plainWhat: Your site's rules file for search engines (its "robots.txt") doesn't give your sitemap's address.
The check found the sitemap anyway, where search engines look first, so most will find it too.
Naming it in the rules file makes sure every search engine does, wherever the sitemap is.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for an option to add the sitemap to the "robots.txt" file.
Ask your developer to add a line to the "robots.txt" file that names your sitemap's full address, if there's no such option.
robots-txt-no-sitemap.plainPassed: Your rules file for search engines names your sitemap

sitemap-over-limit.plainTitle: A sitemap too big for Google to read
plainWhat: A sitemap on your site lists more than 50,000 addresses, or is bigger than 50 MB.
That's more than one sitemap file may hold, and search engines may not read the addresses past the limit.
Those pages then aren't put forward to search engines by the sitemap.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for the number of addresses in each sitemap, and lower it.
Ask your developer to split the sitemap into several smaller ones, listed in one sitemap of sitemaps, if there's no such setting.
sitemap-over-limit.plainPassed: No sitemap is too big for search engines to read

sitemap-near-limit.plainTitle: A sitemap close to the size Google can read
plainWhat: A sitemap on your site lists between 45,000 and 50,000 addresses, or is nearly 50 MB.
That's close to what one sitemap file may hold, and nothing is lost yet.
As you add pages it will pass the limit, and search engines may then not read the addresses past it.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for the number of addresses in each sitemap, and lower it.
Ask your developer to split the sitemap into several smaller ones before it grows, if there's no such setting.
sitemap-near-limit.plainPassed: No sitemap is close to the size search engines can read

sitemap-empty.plainTitle: A sitemap with nothing in it
plainWhat: A sitemap on your site loads without an error but lists no pages.
That does no harm by itself, but it usually means a sitemap that should list pages doesn't.
Or it's an old one left behind, which search engines keep fetching for nothing.
plainFix: Open the sitemap's address from the list in your browser, to see what's in it.
Check your site's SEO settings or plugin, in case that part of the sitemap is switched off.
If the sitemap isn't needed, ask your developer to remove it and the line that names it.

sitemap-url-repeated.plainTitle: Addresses listed in more than one sitemap
plainWhat: These pages are listed in more than one of your sitemaps.
Search engines cope with that, so this is tidying rather than a problem.
Repeats make sitemaps bigger, and the copies can disagree about when a page last changed.
plainFix: Look for two SEO plugins or settings that both make a sitemap, and switch one off.
Otherwise keep each page in the one sitemap for its kind of page.
sitemap-url-repeated.plainPassed: No page is listed in more than one sitemap

plainWhat: Your sitemap gives some pages a last-changed date that isn't a date, or that hasn't happened yet.
Google uses these dates only when they're accurate, so it may ignore them all.
Pages you change may then show up changed in search later.
plainFix: Check your site's SEO settings or plugin: most fill in each page's real last-changed date when left to themselves.
Ask your developer to correct the dates, if your sitemap is made some other way.
sitemap-lastmod-invalid.plainPassed: Every sitemap date is a real date in the past

plainWhat: These pages have no title: the text on the browser tab, and the link people click in search results.
Google has to make one up from other text on the page, which may not say what you'd choose.
Every page should have one, so fix these first.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and fill in its title, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write a title that says what the page is about, and add your site's name if there's room.
If a whole kind of page has no title, ask your developer to set it in the page design.

title-multiple.plainTitle: Pages with more than one title
plainWhat: These pages have more than one title in their code, where only one is allowed.
Browsers use the first, but search engines may use another, so the title you wrote may not be the one shown.
It usually means two parts of your site each write one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page gets a single title.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a title to the page.
title-multiple.plainPassed: No page has more than one title

title-too-long.plainTitle: Titles that may be cut off in search results
plainWhat: These pages have a title too long to show in full in search results, where there's room for {limit:titleMaxPixels}.
Search results cut a long title off to fit the screen, so the last words may not show.
That's harmless when the important words come first, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its title.
Move the words that matter most to the front.
Cut repeated words and long endings, such as a slogan after your site's name.
title-too-long.plainPassed: No title is likely to be cut off in search results

plainWhat: These pages have a title shorter than {limit:titleMinPixels}.
Titles like "Login" or "Products" don't tell a searcher what the page is, or whose.
A short title can be exactly right, such as a product name, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its title.
Say what the page is about, and add your site's name if there's room.
Leave the titles that already say it all.
Skip pages nobody searches for, such as login and basket pages.

title-duplicate.plainTitle: Pages that share the same title
plainWhat: Two or more pages have the same title: the text on the browser tab, and the link people click in search results.
Searchers can't tell the pages apart, and Google may make up a title of its own.
It often means two addresses show the same page, or the site's design leaves out what's different, such as the page number.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and give it a title that says what's specific to it.
If two addresses show the same page, keep one and ask your developer to forward the other to it.
If they differ only by what follows a "?", such as /login/ and /login/?register=true, they're one page, so don't write a new title.
Instead, ask your developer to point the longer address at the shorter one (a "canonical tag"), or to keep it out of search results.
title-duplicate.plainPassed: No two pages share a title

plainWhat: These pages have no search description: the short text under a page's title in search results.
Without one (a "meta description"), Google picks some text from the page, which may not be what you'd choose.
It doesn't change where the page ranks, so start with the pages you most want people to click.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find the description box, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write one or two sentences that say what the page offers.
Skip pages nobody searches for, such as login and basket pages.
description-missing.plainPassed: Every page has a search description

description-multiple.plainTitle: Pages with more than one search description
plainWhat: These pages have more than one search description in their code, where only one is allowed.
Search engines may read either one (each is a "meta description"), so the text you wrote may not be the one used.
It usually means two parts of your site each add one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page gets a single description.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a description to the page.
description-multiple.plainPassed: No page has more than one search description

description-too-long.plainTitle: Search descriptions that may be cut off
plainWhat: These pages have a search description, the text under their title in search results, too long to show in full.
Search results have room for {limit:descriptionMaxPixels}, and cut off the end of a longer description (a "meta description").
That's harmless when the important words come first, so only pages where the cut loses the point need changing.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO".
Put what matters in the first sentence.
Trim the rest to {limit:descriptionMaxPixels}, or leave it if the opening already works.
description-too-long.plainPassed: No search description is likely to be cut off

plainWhat: These pages have a search description, the text under their title in search results, shorter than {limit:descriptionMinPixels}.
One that short (a "meta description") rarely says enough, so Google often shows text from the page instead.
A short one that says everything that matters is fine, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO".
Write one or two sentences that say what the page offers, and who it's for.
description-too-short.plainPassed: No search description is very short

description-duplicate.plainTitle: Pages that share the same search description
plainWhat: Two or more pages share one search description: the short text under a page's title in search results.
Searchers can't tell the pages apart, and Google tends to write its own text instead.
The shared text (a "meta description") often comes from a default that the site's design fills in.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write one or two sentences that say what's on that page and nowhere else.
Leave numbered pages of one list (page 2, page 3) until last: they matter least.
description-duplicate.plainPassed: No two pages share a search description
description-duplicate.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a default description that your page design or SEO plugin gives to pages without one of their own.

plainWhat: These pages have no main heading (an "H1"): the headline that says what the page is about.
People using a screen reader rely on headings to find their way, and the page is harder to scan.
Often the headline is there to look at, but isn't marked as a heading.
It matters more to readers than to search, so it can wait until you next edit the page.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor.
Select the headline at the top and set its style to "Heading 1".
If the headline is part of the page design, ask your developer to mark it as the H1.
h1-missing.plainPassed: Every page has a main heading
h1-missing.plainOneFix: If these pages share one page design, marking its headline as the main heading fixes them all.

h1-multiple.plainTitle: Pages with more than one main heading
plainWhat: These pages have more than one main heading (an "H1"), where one headline for the page is clearest.
Google says this doesn't matter for search, so it's about readers: screen readers use the main heading to say what the page is.
Often the page design marks the logo or a side panel's title as a main heading too.
The gain is small, so it can wait.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and see which lines are set to "Heading 1".
Keep that style for the page's headline, and set the others to "Heading 2" or plain text.
If the extra one is the logo or part of the page design, ask your developer to change it there.
h1-multiple.plainPassed: No page has more than one main heading

h1-duplicate.plainTitle: Pages that share the same main heading
plainWhat: Two or more pages have the same main heading (an "H1"): the headline that says what the page is about.
Visitors who land on one can't tell it from the other, and it often means the pages themselves are copies.
If the pages are clearly different in every other way, there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and look at its headline.
Change it to say what's specific to that page, such as the product, place or topic.
If two addresses show the same page, keep one and ask your developer to forward the other to it.
h1-duplicate.plainPassed: No two pages share a main heading
h1-duplicate.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one heading in your page design, such as your site's name, marked as the main heading of every page.

plainWhat: These pages have headings that jump a level, such as a main section heading followed by a sub-sub-heading.
People who use screen readers move through a page by its headings, and a jump suggests a section is missing.
plainFix: Edit each page and use the next heading size down for each smaller section.
Change how a heading looks with your site's styles, not by picking a smaller heading.
heading-levels-skipped.plainPassed: No page's headings jump a level

plainWhat: These pages' main heading is a picture, such as your logo, with no words of its own.
It says the same on every page, your site's name, rather than what the page is about.
plainFix: Give each page a main heading in words that says what the page is about.
Keep the logo as a picture beside it, or elsewhere on the page.
h1-image-only.plainPassed: Every main heading is in words

plainWhat: These pages have a main heading or section heading longer than {limit:headingMaxLength}.
A long heading is harder to take in at a glance, and on a phone it wraps over several lines.
plainFix: Shorten each heading to what the section is about, and move the rest into the text below it.

plainWhat: These long pages have no subheadings to break up their text.
Readers find it hard to scan a long page without them, and to find the part they want.
plainFix: Divide each page's text into sections, each under a subheading that says what it covers.

plainWhat: These pages have fewer than {limit:minWordCount} of their own, not counting menus and footers.
Short pages are often fine, and then there's nothing to do: a contact page doesn't need an essay.
This list is for spotting pages that are empty by mistake, such as one where the content failed to appear.
plainFix: Open each page and see whether anything is missing.
If content is missing, put it back.
If the page is meant to be short, leave it.
low-word-count.plainPassed: No page has very little text

plainWhat: Two or more pages have exactly the same main text, word for word.
Google shows only one of them, and it may not be the one you'd choose.
Usually it's one page that can be reached at several addresses, such as a print version or an address with extras on the end.
plainFix: Open the pages in each group and decide which address is the one you want found.
Ask your developer to forward the other addresses to it (a "301 redirect"), or to name it as their main address (a "canonical" link).
If the pages are meant to differ, give each one text of its own.
duplicate-content.plainPassed: No two pages have identical content

plainWhat: Two or more pages have almost the same main text: only a few words differ.
Google may treat them as copies and show only one.
That's fine for versions you don't need found separately, such as one product in several sizes, and then there's nothing to do.
Pages that should each be found, such as one per town, need text that is clearly their own.
plainFix: Open the pages in each group side by side and decide whether each needs to be found on its own.
If so, give each page text that is clearly its own.
If not, ask your developer to name one of them as the main version (a "canonical" link), or merge them into one page.
near-duplicate-content.plainPassed: No two pages have almost identical content

duplicate-site-version.plainTitle: Your site answers at more than one address
duplicate-site-version.plainLooksFor: A site that answers at more than one address
plainWhat: Your site shows its pages at more than one address, such as with and without "www", or on "http" as well as "https".
The spare addresses should forward to the main one.
As it is, search engines see two copies of everything and pick one themselves.
Visitors on an "http" copy also browse without encryption.
plainFix: Decide which address is the main one: usually the "https" one your home page uses.
Ask your developer or hosting company to forward every other version to it (a "301 redirect"), page for page.
Check the site again to confirm.
duplicate-site-version.plainPassed: The site answers at one address only

plainWhat: These pages have the dummy text "lorem ipsum" on them, which designers use until the real words are written.
Every visitor sees it, and the site looks unfinished, and Google may show it under the page in search.
plainFix: Replace the dummy text with the page's real words, or remove the part it's in.
Check other pages made from the same design for it too.

readability-low.plainTitle: Writing that's very hard to read
plainWhat: These pages' English text uses long sentences of long words, which makes it very hard to read.
Many readers give up before they reach the point, on phones above all.
plainFix: Shorten long sentences, split ones that say several things, and use everyday words where they mean the same.

boilerplate-heavy.plainTitle: Pages that are mostly menus and footers
plainWhat: Less than a quarter of the words on these pages are their own: the rest are menus, footers and sidebars.
Search engines see little on them that's different from your other pages.
plainFix: Add more of each page's own text about what it offers.
Trim menus and footers that repeat long lists of links on every page.
boilerplate-heavy.plainPassed: Every page has enough words of its own

plainWhat: Some images on these pages have no description: the short text that says what an image shows.
People who can't see the image rely on it, and Google uses it to understand the image for image search.
An image that is only decoration needs no words, but should be marked as decoration so screen readers skip it.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor, select each image and fill in its description box, often called "Alt text".
Say what the image shows, in a few words, as you would to someone who can't see it.
Ask your developer to do the same for images in the page design, and to mark decoration as such (an empty "alt").
image-missing-alt.plainPassed: No image is missing its description

image-alt-too-long.plainTitle: Image descriptions that are too long
plainWhat: Some images on these pages have a description, the text that says what an image shows, of more than {limit:imageAltMaxLength}.
A screen reader reads the whole description aloud in one go, and its user can't skim it.
The limit is a rule of thumb, so a description just over it that reads well is fine to leave.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor, select the image and find its description box, often called "Alt text".
Cut it to a short phrase that says what the image shows.
Move longer detail, such as the figures in a chart, into a caption or the text beside the image.
image-alt-too-long.plainPassed: No image description is too long

image-missing-dimensions.plainTitle: Images with no width and height set
plainWhat: Some images on these pages don't tell the browser their width and height.
The browser may not leave the right space, so text can jump down the page as each image arrives.
That annoys readers and counts against the page in Google's speed measures.
If your site's design already sets the size another way, there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open one of the pages on a phone and watch whether the text jumps as the images appear.
If it does, ask your developer to add a width and height to the images in the page design.
image-missing-dimensions.plainPassed: No image is missing its width and height

plainWhat: Some images on these pages don't load: the image file can't be found, or fails with an error.
Visitors see a gap or a broken-image icon, which makes the page look unfinished.
An image in the page design, such as a logo, shows broken on every page that uses it.
plainFix: Open one of the pages in your browser and look for the gap where the image should be.
Upload the image again in your site's editor, or choose another one.
Remove the image from the page if it's no longer needed.
Ask your developer to fix it in the page design if the same image is missing on most pages.
image-broken.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly an image in your page design, such as a logo or icon, which every page shares.

image-too-large.plainTitle: Large images that slow pages down
plainWhat: Some pages show images whose files are over {limit:largeImageBytes}.
Big images are the most common reason a page feels slow, most of all on a phone, and people leave slow pages.
Photos uploaded straight from a camera or phone are the usual cause.
plainFix: Resize each image so it's no bigger than it's shown on the page.
Save it as a compressed JPEG or WebP, then upload it in place of the old one.
If your site has an image-optimising setting or plugin, turn it on so new uploads are shrunk for you.
image-too-large.plainPassed: No image is too big to load quickly

image-missing-src.plainTitle: Images with no picture file named
plainWhat: These pages have image spaces that don't say which picture to show.
Nothing appears there, for visitors or in Google's image search.
It's usually an empty slot in a page design, or code that fills pictures in a way that isn't standard.
plainFix: Open each page and find the empty picture space.
Choose a picture for it in your site's editor, or remove the empty space.
Ask your developer to check how pictures are loaded, if every page has the problem.
image-missing-src.plainPassed: Every image names its picture file

image-no-srcset.plainTitle: Big images sent to phones at full size
plainWhat: These pages show pictures at least {limit:responsiveImageMinWidth} wide, with no smaller versions for small screens.
Phones then download the whole picture, which makes the page slower and uses visitors' data.
plainFix: Upload these pictures through your site's media library, which usually makes smaller versions for phones.
Ask your developer to offer smaller versions of each picture, if your site doesn't.
image-no-srcset.plainPassed: Big images come in smaller versions for phones

image-legacy-format.plainTitle: Images that could be smaller in a newer format
plainWhat: These pages show pictures of {limit:legacyImageMinBytes} or more saved in an older format, such as JPEG or PNG.
Newer formats (WebP or AVIF) usually make the same picture a quarter to a half smaller, so pages load faster.
plainFix: Look for an image optimisation setting or plugin that converts pictures to WebP.
Or save the pictures as WebP before you upload them.
image-legacy-format.plainPassed: No large image is in an older format

image-alt-unhelpful.plainTitle: Image descriptions that don't describe anything
plainWhat: These pages have pictures whose descriptions are a file name, a camera's number such as "IMG_1234", or a stray letter.
People using screen readers hear that instead of what the picture shows, and Google learns nothing from it.
plainFix: Edit each picture in your site's media library and describe what it shows in a few words.
Leave the description empty for a picture that's only decoration.

image-hotlinked.plainTitle: Images shown straight from other websites
plainWhat: These pages show pictures that are stored on other websites, not on yours.
They can disappear or change whenever the other site moves them, and use that site's resources.
plainFix: Check you're allowed to use each picture.
Download the ones you may use and upload them to your own site, then show them from there.
image-hotlinked.plainPassed: Every image is shown from your own site

image-inline-large.plainTitle: Pictures built into the page that slow it down
plainWhat: These pages have pictures of more than {limit:inlineImageMaxBytes} written into the page itself, not kept as separate files.
They come with the page on every visit and can't be saved by the browser, so every view is slower.
plainFix: Ask your developer to save these pictures as ordinary image files and link to them instead.
image-inline-large.plainPassed: No large picture is built into a page

hreflang-invalid-code.plainTitle: Language versions labelled with an invalid code
plainWhat: These pages list their versions in other languages, but label one with an invalid language or country code.
Google ignores that entry (an "hreflang" link), or reads only its language, so searchers may be shown the wrong version.
A common slip is "en-UK": the code for the United Kingdom is "GB".
plainFix: Look at the codes the list shows for each page.
Send the list to your developer and ask for each code in the form language, then country, such as "en-GB" or "de-AT".
Ask them to correct it on every page that lists the same versions, not only the ones shown here.
hreflang-invalid-code.plainPassed: No language version is labelled with an invalid code
hreflang-invalid-code.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

hreflang-missing-self.plainTitle: Language versions that don't list themselves
plainWhat: These pages list their versions in other languages, but leave their own address out of the list.
Google expects every version to name itself as well as the others, and may ignore a list that doesn't.
Often the page is in its list, but written slightly differently, such as "http" for "https" or without the final slash.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: this is a change to the code of your pages.
Ask them to add each page's own address to its list of language versions (its "hreflang" links).
Ask them to write it exactly as the page is addressed, with the same "https", "www" and final slash.
hreflang-missing-self.plainPassed: No language version leaves itself out of its list

hreflang-missing-return.plainTitle: Language versions that don't link back
plainWhat: These pages name versions in other languages that don't name them back.
Google needs both pages to agree before it trusts the pairing, so searchers may be shown the wrong language.
It usually means a new language was added to some pages' lists but not to others.
plainFix: Open one of the pages and a version it names, to confirm that both exist.
Send the list to your developer and ask them to give every version the same full list (of "hreflang" links).
Ask them to make sure each list includes the page itself, at its exact address.
hreflang-missing-return.plainPassed: No language version is missing its link back
hreflang-missing-return.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one entry in the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

hreflang-broken-target.plainTitle: Language versions that lead to a broken page
plainWhat: These pages list a version in another language at an address that doesn't work.
Searchers sent to that version get an error, and the entry for that language does nothing.
Usually the version was removed or moved, and the lists (of "hreflang" links) were never updated.
plainFix: Open the broken address the list shows in your browser, to see the error.
If that version has moved, ask your developer to point the entry at its new address.
If it's gone, ask them to remove the entry from every page that lists it.
