hreflang-broken-target.plainPassed: No language version leads to a broken page
hreflang-broken-target.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one entry in the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

hreflang-to-non-indexable.plainTitle: Language versions that search engines can't show
plainWhat: These pages list a version in another language at an address that can't itself appear in search results.
That address forwards elsewhere, is kept out of search, names another page as its main version, or is blocked by your rules file ("robots.txt").
Search engines can't show it, so the entry for that language (an "hreflang" link) can't be relied on.
plainFix: Open the address the list shows in your browser, and see whether it moves you on to a different address.
If it does, ask your developer to list that final address instead.
If it doesn't, ask them to list a version that can appear in search, or to let that one appear.
hreflang-to-non-indexable.plainPassed: No language version leads to a page search can't show
hreflang-to-non-indexable.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one entry in the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

hreflang-duplicate-code.plainTitle: Two addresses listed for the same language
hreflang-duplicate-code.plainLooksFor: Languages listed at more than one address
plainWhat: These pages list two or more different addresses for the same language or country.
Search engines can't tell which one to show searchers in that language.
It usually means two parts of your site each add a list (of "hreflang" links), such as a plugin and the page design.
plainFix: Look at the codes the list shows: each is a language that has more than one address.
Check whether your site has two translation or SEO plugins that each add language versions, and turn one off.
Ask your developer to keep one address for each language, if the lists are written in the page design.
hreflang-duplicate-code.plainPassed: No language is listed at two different addresses
hreflang-duplicate-code.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly the list of language versions in your page design, which every page shares.

hreflang-missing-x-default.plainTitle: Language versions with no fallback page
plainWhat: These pages list their versions in other languages, but name no fallback for everyone else.
The fallback (called "x-default") is the page search engines show when a searcher's language isn't in the list.
Google suggests one but doesn't require it, so if your versions cover your visitors there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Pick the page for visitors whose language you don't cover: usually your language chooser or your main version.
Ask your developer to add it to every page's list of language versions, labelled "x-default".
hreflang-missing-x-default.plainPassed: No list of language versions is missing a fallback page

hreflang-outside-head.plainTitle: Language versions written in the wrong part of the page
plainWhat: These pages list some or all of their language versions in a part of the page where search engines ignore them.
The entries there (they're "hreflang" links) don't count, so searchers may be shown the wrong language.
It usually means something added near the top of the page's code, by a plugin or script, has pushed them out of place.
plainFix: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately, as one of them may be the cause.
Send the list to your developer: the hreflang links must sit in the page's "head" section.
Ask them to move or remove whatever ends that section early.
hreflang-outside-head.plainPassed: No language version is written in the wrong part of the page

hreflang-inconsistent-code.plainTitle: Language versions that disagree about their language
plainWhat: These pages point to another language version of themselves, but name its language differently from it.
Google may then ignore the language settings and show the wrong version.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the two names each pair uses.
Ask for every version to use the same language name for each page, the one the page uses for itself.
hreflang-inconsistent-code.plainPassed: Every language version agrees on its language

hreflang-header-mismatch.plainTitle: Language versions listed two different ways
plainWhat: These pages list their other language versions twice, in the page and in its server settings, and the two lists differ.
Google can't tell which list is right.
plainFix: Ask your developer to list the language versions in one place only, or to make both lists the same.
hreflang-header-mismatch.plainPassed: Language versions are listed one consistent way

hreflang-unlinked.plainTitle: Language versions that nothing links to
plainWhat: These pages are another page's version in another language, but no page on your site links to them.
Visitors can't reach them, and search engines see them as less important.
plainFix: Add a language switcher, or links between each page's language versions.
List these pages in your sitemap too.
hreflang-unlinked.plainPassed: Every language version has links to it

hreflang-lang-mismatch.plainTitle: Pages that name two different languages
plainWhat: These pages give one language in their settings for search engines and another in their page code.
One of them is usually wrong, copied from another language version unchanged.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the two languages each page names.
Ask them to correct whichever one is wrong.

hreflang-self-only.plainTitle: Language settings that list no other language
plainWhat: These pages have language settings for search engines that list only the page itself.
They do nothing on their own: they only help when they point to versions in other languages.
plainFix: If your site has other language versions, list them all on every version.
If it has none, ask your developer to remove the language settings.
hreflang-self-only.plainPassed: Every page's language settings list its other versions

structured-data-invalid.plainTitle: Details for search engines that can't be read
plainWhat: Some pages carry details for search engines, such as a product's price, in code that has a mistake in it.
Google ignores the broken details (they're called "structured data"), so the page may lose extras such as star ratings in its results.
One mistake in the page design usually breaks it on every page of that kind.
plainFix: Test one of the pages in Google's Rich Results Test, a free tool on the web, to see the error.
Send the list to your developer: it shows the first error in each page's code (a "JSON-LD" block).
Ask them to fix the page design that writes it, then test the page again.
structured-data-invalid.plainPassed: No details for search engines have a mistake in them
structured-data-invalid.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one mistake in your page design, which writes the same code on every page.

structured-data-missing-required.plainTitle: Details for search engines with parts missing
plainWhat: Some pages describe a product, event or similar for search engines, but leave out a detail Google requires.
Without it, Google won't add the extras to your search result, such as stars, prices or dates (a "rich result").
Even complete details only make the extras possible: Google decides whether to show them.
plainFix: Look at what the list says is missing on each page, such as "Product: needs name".
Fill in that detail in your site's editor or shop settings if it's something you enter, such as a price or a date.
If it isn't, ask your developer to add it to the page's "structured data", then test the page in Google's Rich Results Test.
structured-data-missing-required.plainPassed: No details for search engines are missing a needed part
structured-data-missing-required.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly your page design, which leaves the same detail out of every page of one kind.

structured-data-schema-errors.plainTitle: Product or business details Google can't use
plainWhat: These pages describe a product, article or business for search engines in words that code doesn't have.
Search engines quietly ignore what they can't read, so those details may do nothing for the page.
A misspelt name such as "Organisation", or a date or currency written the wrong way, is the usual cause.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the first few mistakes on each page.
If a plugin writes these details, check its settings for dates and currencies, or update it.
structured-data-schema-errors.plainPassed: All product and business details use words Google knows

structured-data-missing-recommended.plainTitle: Product or article details that could be fuller
plainWhat: These pages describe a product, an article or your business for search engines, but leave out details Google asks for.
Nothing is broken, but Google uses them to show more in search, such as an article's picture or a product's price and stock.
A product needs a picture to be shown in Google's shopping results at all.
plainFix: Check the list: it says what each page leaves out.
Fill in the missing details in your site's SEO or shop settings, such as an article's featured image or a product's stock.
Ask your developer to add them, if your site has no such settings.
structured-data-missing-recommended.plainPassed: Every product and article gives the details Google asks for

structured-data-on-noindex.plainTitle: Product or article details on pages hidden from Google
plainWhat: These pages describe a product or an article for search engines, but also ask not to be shown in search.
Google can't show those details for a page it leaves out, so they do nothing here.
It's harmless, but often a sign that a page meant to be found is hidden by mistake.
plainFix: Check whether each page should appear in search results.
If it should, switch off "hide from search engines" for it in your site's settings.
If it shouldn't, there's nothing to do.
structured-data-on-noindex.plainPassed: No hidden page carries product or article details

no-https.plainLooksFor: A site that isn't secure (no HTTPS)
plainWhat: Your site doesn't use HTTPS, the secure connection, so nothing sent to or from it is protected.
Browsers label every page "Not secure", and anything a visitor types, such as a password, can be read on the way.
Google prefers the secure version of a page when it has the choice.
This is one fault for the whole site, and the first thing to fix.
plainFix: Open your site with "https://" in front of its address, to see whether a secure version already exists.
Ask your hosting company to switch on HTTPS: most include a free certificate.
Ask them, or your developer, to forward every "http" address to its "https" version (a "301 redirect").
Check the site again, and update any links and settings that still say "http".

http-page.plainTitle: Pages still on the insecure address
plainWhat: These pages still load over "http", without the secure connection the rest of your site uses.
Browsers label them "Not secure", and if an "https" copy exists too, search engines see two copies of the page.
Usually an old link or sitemap entry still points at the "http" address, and nothing forwards it on.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser and look for "Not secure" beside it.
Ask your developer or hosting company to forward every "http" address to its "https" version (a "301 redirect").
Change the links and sitemap entries that still use "http", so they point at the "https" address.
http-page.plainPassed: No page is left on the insecure address

mixed-content.plainTitle: Secure pages that load insecure files
plainWhat: These secure pages load some of their files, such as images or scripts, over an insecure "http" address.
Browsers block some of these files (they call it "mixed content"), so parts of the page can break or go missing.
It's usually an old "http" address left in the page or its design.
plainFix: Open one of the pages in your browser and look for missing images, or a warning beside the address.
Change each address the list shows from "http" to "https", in your site's editor.
If the file is in your page design, ask your developer to change it there.
If the other site has no "https" version, copy the file to your own site or replace it.
mixed-content.plainPassed: No secure page loads an insecure file
mixed-content.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a file your page design loads on every page, such as a script, style file or logo.

plainWhat: Your site doesn't send some of the settings that tell browsers how to protect visitors (its "security headers").
They guard against attacks such as someone showing your site inside a fake one.
Only your home page is checked, as these are set once for the whole site.
Search isn't affected and many sites run without them, so this can wait until your developer next works on the site.
plainFix: Send this to your developer or hosting company: the list names the missing settings.
Ask them to add the simple ones first (X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy), and to test the others before switching them on.
security-headers-missing.plainPassed: No recommended security setting is missing

security-headers-weak.plainTitle: Security settings that are on but too weak
plainWhat: Your site sends some security settings to browsers, but sets them too weakly to do their job.
One that keeps visitors on the secure version of your site may lapse between visits, for example.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer or hosting company: it says which settings are too weak.
Ask them to strengthen each one, as the list describes.
security-headers-weak.plainPassed: Your site's security settings are strong enough

cookies-insecure.plainTitle: Cookies your site sets without basic protection
plainWhat: These pages store small files in visitors' browsers (cookies) without the basic protections browsers offer.
A login cookie without them could be read by someone else, which is how accounts get taken over.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it names each cookie and what it lacks.
Ask them to turn on the cookie protections in your site's settings or code.

form-not-secure.plainTitle: Forms that send what people type without encryption
plainWhat: These pages have forms that send what people type over an unencrypted connection.
Others on the same network could read it, and browsers warn visitors before they send it.
plainFix: Ask your developer to make each form send to a secure address, one that starts with https.
If a form plugin made the form, check its settings for the address it sends to.

protocol-relative-links.plainTitle: Links written in an old shortcut style
plainWhat: These pages load files or link to addresses written without their start ("//" instead of "https://").
That shortcut was once common, and still works on a secure page, but it's best replaced.
plainFix: Ask your developer to write each address in full, starting with "https://".
protocol-relative-links.plainPassed: Every address is written in full

plainWhat: These pages have capital letters in their address, such as /About-Us.
Capitals count in an address: /Page and /page are two different addresses, so a link typed in small letters can miss.
An address that works and is always linked the same way is fine to leave, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Use small letters only in the address of every new page.
Leave an existing address alone unless it causes broken links or copies of the page.
If it does, ask your developer to forward it to the small-letter version (a "301 redirect"), and update your links.
url-uppercase.plainPassed: No page address has capital letters

plainWhat: These pages have underscores in their address, such as /garden_chairs.
Google recommends hyphens instead, as in /garden-chairs, because it reads them as gaps between words.
The gain is small, so there's nothing to do for addresses that already exist.
plainFix: Use hyphens between words in the address of every new page.
Leave existing addresses alone, unless you're changing them for another reason.
If you do change one, ask your developer to forward the old address to the new one (a "301 redirect").

plainWhat: These pages have an address of more than {limit:maxUrlLength}.
Search isn't affected, but long addresses are harder to read, share and type.
They often come from folders inside folders, or from tracking codes added to links.
An address that works is fine to leave, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Keep the address short and readable when you make a new page.
Remove tracking codes, such as "?utm_source=newsletter", from links between your own pages.
Leave existing addresses alone, or ask your developer to forward the old address if you shorten one (a "301 redirect").
url-too-long.plainPassed: No page address is very long

url-tracking-parameters.plainTitle: Links between your own pages tagged for ad tracking
plainWhat: Some of your pages link to others with tracking codes meant for ads and emails in the address.
Each such link is another address for search engines, and it muddles your visitor statistics.
plainFix: Find the links on the pages the list names, and remove the tracking codes after the "?" from each address.
url-tracking-parameters.plainPassed: No link between your own pages is tagged for tracking

plainWhat: These pages' addresses have two slashes in a row.
That makes them different addresses from the single-slash ones, so search engines may see two copies.
plainFix: Change the links to these pages to use a single slash.
Ask your developer to forward each double-slash address to the single-slash one.
url-multiple-slashes.plainPassed: No address has a double slash

plainWhat: These pages' addresses have a space in them, which addresses can't hold as typed.
It shows as "%20", reads badly, and breaks when the address is copied into emails.
plainFix: Rename each page with hyphens in place of the spaces, in your site's editor.
Ask your developer to forward the old addresses to the new ones.
url-space.plainPassed: No address has a space in it

url-parameters.plainTitle: Pages whose address has a ? part
plainWhat: These pages can appear in search, and their addresses have a "?" part, as sorting and filtering often add.
Each different "?" part is another address for search engines to visit, often for the same content.
plainFix: Check whether each page is worth finding in search on its own.
If not, ask your developer to point its main address at the version without the "?" part.
url-parameters.plainPassed: No page that can appear in search has a ? part

url-non-ascii.plainTitle: Addresses with accented or non-English letters
plainWhat: These pages' addresses have accented or non-English letters in them.
Search engines read them fine, but they turn into long codes when copied, which some people and tools get wrong.
plainFix: Use plain letters, hyphens and numbers in new page addresses.
Don't rename pages that already do well in search.

plainWhat: These addresses repeat part of themselves, such as "/shop/shop/".
It's usually a link written slightly wrong, which builds ever-longer addresses for search engines to follow.
plainFix: Look at the pages the list names for the link that leads here.
Ask your developer to correct the link and forward the address to the right page.

url-internal-search.plainTitle: Your site's search results pages show up as pages
plainWhat: Search engines can find and show your site's own search results pages.
They rarely help anyone arriving from a search engine, and there's no end of them to visit.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for an option to hide search results from search engines.
Avoid linking to search results from your own pages.
url-internal-search.plainPassed: Your site's search results stay out of search engines

slow-response.plainTitle: Pages that are slow to answer
plainWhat: These pages took more than {limit:slowResponseMs} to arrive when the check asked for them.
Nothing can appear on screen until the page arrives, so visitors wait, and Google visits slow sites less often.
One slow reading can be a blip, so try the pages yourself before acting.
plainFix: Open two or three of the pages in your browser and see whether they're slow for you too.
If they are, send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask what the server is waiting for.
Ask about page caching and a faster hosting plan: they're the usual fixes.
slow-response.plainPassed: No page is slow to answer

large-page.plainTitle: Pages with a lot of code to download
plainWhat: These pages have more than {limit:largePageBytes} of code in the page itself, before any images or other files.
A page that heavy takes longer to arrive and to appear, most of all on a phone.
Google also stops reading a page at 2 MB, which is listed as a problem of its own.
Below 2 MB, a page that still feels quick on a phone needs nothing done.
plainFix: Open one of the pages on a phone and see whether it's slow to appear.
If it is, send the list to your developer: it shows each page's size.
Ask them to move scripts, styles and images that are written into the page out into separate files, and to split very long lists.
large-page.plainPassed: No page has too much code to download

html-past-crawl-limit.plainTitle: Pages too big for Google to read in full
plainWhat: These pages have more than 2 MB of code in the page itself, which is as far as Google reads.
Google ignores everything after that point, so text and links near the end of the page aren't seen.
The bulk is usually scripts, styles or images written into the page instead of loaded as separate files.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it shows each page's size.
Ask them to move scripts, styles and images that are written into the page out into separate files.
Ask them to put the main text and links early in the page, within the first 2 MB.
html-past-crawl-limit.plainPassed: No page is too big for Google to read in full

resource-past-crawl-limit.plainTitle: Code files too big for Google to read in full
plainWhat: These code or style files are bigger than the part of each file Google reads.
Google ignores the rest, so it may see your pages without some of their look or how they work.
Files that big also make pages slow on phones.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer, with the size of each file.
Ask them to split each file, or to remove what your pages don't use.
resource-past-crawl-limit.plainPassed: No code file is too big for Google to read in full

viewport-missing.plainTitle: Pages not set up for phones
plainWhat: These pages lack the line of code that tells a phone to fit the page to its screen.
Phones show them as a tiny copy of the desktop page, so visitors must zoom and scroll sideways to read.
Google reads every page as a phone would, so this is the version it judges.
plainFix: Open one of the pages on a phone and see whether the text is too small to read.
Ask your developer to add the missing line (a "viewport" setting) to the page design.
Ask them to check the page design really adapts to small screens, as the line alone won't do it.
viewport-missing.plainPassed: No page is missing its phone-screen setting

lang-missing.plainTitle: Pages that don't say what language they're in
plainWhat: These pages don't state in their code which language they're written in.
Screen readers use that to pick the right voice, so without it they may read the page in the wrong accent.
Google works the language out from the text itself, so search isn't affected and this can wait.
plainFix: Check your site's settings for a "site language" option, and set it if it's empty.
Ask your developer to add the language to the page design (a "lang" setting, such as "en-GB") if there's no such option.
lang-missing.plainPassed: Every page says what language it is in

charset-missing.plainTitle: Pages at risk of showing garbled characters
plainWhat: These pages don't tell browsers how their letters and symbols were saved, or tell them too far down the page.
Browsers have to guess, and a wrong guess turns accents, £ signs and curly quotes into nonsense.
Pages that look right today can wait, but the one-line fix removes the risk.
plainFix: Open one of the pages and look for odd symbols where accents, £ signs or quote marks should be.
Ask your developer to state the character set in the page design (a "charset" line, set to "utf-8").
charset-missing.plainPassed: No page leaves browsers guessing its characters

open-graph-missing.plainTitle: Pages that won't preview well when shared
plainWhat: These pages lack the title, description or image that apps show when someone shares a link.
Without them (they're called "Open Graph tags"), the preview is a guess, or a bare link.
It matters only for pages people are likely to share: for the rest there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Find the page's "social sharing" or "social preview" settings in your site's editor.
Add a title, a short description and an image.
If there's no such setting, ask your developer to add Open Graph tags to the page design.
open-graph-missing.plainPassed: Every page has its sharing preview details
open-graph-missing.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly your page design, which leaves the same details out of every page.

x-card-missing.plainTitle: Pages without a preview card for X
plainWhat: These pages don't say which kind of preview X (Twitter) should show when someone shares them.
X then shows a plain link, or a small preview, instead of a card with a picture.
plainFix: Turn on X (Twitter) cards in your SEO plugin or theme settings.
If there's no setting, ask your developer to add an X card to every page.
x-card-missing.plainPassed: Every page has a preview card for X

x-card-incomplete.plainTitle: Preview cards for X that are missing parts
plainWhat: These pages ask X (Twitter) for a preview card, but leave out something the card needs, such as a title or a picture.
X can't build the card, so people see a plain link instead.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it says what each page's card lacks.
Ask them to fill in the missing parts, or to write the card the way X reads it.
x-card-incomplete.plainPassed: Every preview card for X is complete

social-image-relative.plainTitle: Share images given an incomplete address
plainWhat: These pages name the picture to show when they're shared, but give only part of its address.
Facebook, X and others need the full address, so they may show no picture.
plainFix: Ask your developer to give the full address of each share picture, starting with https://.
social-image-relative.plainPassed: Every share picture has its full address

og-url-not-canonical.plainTitle: Share links that point to a different page
plainWhat: These pages tell social networks that their address is another page's, often your home page.
Shares and likes then count toward that page, and people who click the share land there.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it gives the address each page names.
Ask them to make each page name its own address, or leave the setting out.
og-url-not-canonical.plainPassed: Every page names its own address for sharing

social-tags-multiple.plainTitle: Share settings given twice with different values
plainWhat: These pages give the same share setting, such as the title to show, twice, with different words.
Social networks pick one of them, and it may not be the one you want.
plainFix: Look for two plugins or a plugin and your theme both adding share settings, and turn one of them off.
If that isn't it, ask your developer to remove the copy.
social-tags-multiple.plainPassed: No share setting is given twice

og-title-duplicate.plainTitle: Pages that share the same title when shared
plainWhat: These pages have different titles in search, but show the same title when they're shared on social networks.
People who see the shares can't tell the pages apart.
plainFix: Give each page its own share title in your SEO plugin, or leave it empty so the page's own title is used.
og-title-duplicate.plainPassed: Every page has its own share title

og-description-duplicate.plainTitle: Pages that share the same summary when shared
plainWhat: These pages have different summaries in search, but show the same summary when they're shared on social networks.
Each share then says the same thing, whatever the page is about.
plainFix: Give each page its own share summary in your SEO plugin, or leave it empty so the page's own description is used.
og-description-duplicate.plainPassed: Every page has its own share summary

plainWhat: The picture these pages name for social networks doesn't load: it's missing, or it isn't a picture.
Shares of these pages show no picture.
plainFix: Choose a new share picture for each page in your SEO plugin, or upload the missing one again.

social-image-too-large.plainTitle: Share images too big to show
plainWhat: The picture these pages name for social networks is larger than 5 MB.
X won't show a picture that large, and other networks are slow to load it.
plainFix: Save a smaller copy of each picture, under 1 MB is plenty, and choose it as the share picture.
social-image-too-large.plainPassed: No share picture is too big

social-image-too-small.plainTitle: Share images too small to show well
plainWhat: The picture these pages name for social networks is smaller than they need.
Facebook won't use a picture under 200 pixels square, and X shows a small one blurred or not at all.
plainFix: Choose a larger share picture for each page: 1,200 by 630 pixels suits every network.
social-image-too-small.plainPassed: Every share picture is large enough

head-tags-in-body.plainTitle: Page settings that ended up where they're ignored
plainWhat: Some settings these pages give search engines and social sites, such as the title, are where they may be ignored.
Usually something placed too early on the page, such as a banner or a tracking code, pushed them out of place.
The list says which settings moved, and what moved them.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it names what moved the settings on each page.
Ask them to move that item further down the page, or remove it.
head-tags-in-body.plainPassed: Every page setting is where search engines read it
head-tags-in-body.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one item in your page design or a plugin, which every page shares.

html-structure-errors.plainTitle: Pages whose basic HTML structure is broken
plainWhat: The code of these pages has some of its basic parts twice, or out of order.
Browsers fix this the same way every time, so visitors rarely notice, but some settings on the second part are lost.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer: it says what's wrong on each page.
Ask them to fix the page design so each page has its parts once, in order.
html-structure-errors.plainPassed: No page has its basic structure broken

viewport-invalid.plainTitle: Pages people can't zoom, or that don't fit phones
plainWhat: These pages stop visitors zooming in on phones, or don't tell phones how wide to show them.
People who need larger text can't read them, and a page with no width shows tiny on a phone.
plainFix: Ask your developer to set the phone-screen setting to the standard "width=device-width, initial-scale=1", with nothing that limits zoom.
viewport-invalid.plainPassed: Every page lets people zoom and fits phones

charset-invalid.plainTitle: Pages that name the wrong text encoding
plainWhat: These pages say they use a text encoding other than the standard one (UTF-8), or say two different things about it.
Browsers then have to guess, and a wrong guess turns accents, currency signs and quotes into garbled characters.
plainFix: Ask your developer to save and serve every page as UTF-8, and to declare it once, at the top of the page.
charset-invalid.plainPassed: Every page names its text encoding correctly

lang-invalid.plainTitle: Pages that name their language wrongly
plainWhat: These pages give their language as something that isn't a language code, such as "english" or "en_GB".
Screen readers then can't tell which voice to use, so the page may be read out in the wrong accent.
plainFix: Change the page's language setting to a code such as "en" or "en-GB": a hyphen, not an underscore, with the language first.
lang-invalid.plainPassed: Every page names its language correctly

mobile-alternate.plainTitle: Pages with a separate mobile version
plainWhat: These pages point to a separate version of themselves for phones, at another address.
Google still supports that, but a single page that fits every screen is simpler to keep right.
plainFix: Check that each mobile page names this page as its main version.
If you're redesigning, consider one page that fits every screen instead.
mobile-alternate.plainPassed: No page has a separate mobile version

sitemaps-off.plainText: This site check was set not to read sitemaps: the files that list your pages for search engines.
sitemaps-off.plainAction: Switch sitemaps back on in the check's Advanced settings, then check the site again.

crawl-unfinished.plainText: The site check stopped before it finished, so it hasn't seen the whole site.
crawl-unfinished.plainAction: Continue the site check, and let it run to the end.

sitemaps-unfinished.plainText: The site check ended before every sitemap had been read.
sitemaps-unfinished.plainAction: Check the site again, and let it run to the end.

no-sitemap.plainText: No sitemap, the list of your pages for search engines, could be read, so there was nothing to compare with.
no-sitemap.plainAction: Add a sitemap, or fix the one that can't be read, then check the site again.

sitemap-unreadable.plainText: One of your sitemaps couldn't be read, so the check can't tell which pages it lists.
sitemap-unreadable.plainAction: Fix the sitemap that can't be read (it's listed as a serious problem), then check the site again.

sitemaps-not-read.plainText: Your site has more sitemaps than Shouting Iguana reads: over 1,000 of them, or lists of sitemaps more than 3 layers deep.
sitemaps-not-read.plainAction: Leave your site as it is: this version of Shouting Iguana can't run this check on it.

depth-limit.plainText: The site check was set to stop a number of clicks from the start page, so it didn't read the whole site.
depth-limit.plainAction: Remove the depth limit in the check's Advanced settings, then check the site again.

url-limit.plainText: The site check stopped at its limit of addresses, so it didn't read the whole site.
url-limit.plainAction: Check the site again, and choose "The whole site" when you start it.

start-folder.plainText: The site check was kept to one section of the site, so links from the rest of it weren't read.
start-folder.plainAction: Start the check from your home page, so it reads the whole site.

pages-unread.plainText: Your site turned the check away from many of its pages, or they didn't answer, so the links on those pages weren't read.
pages-unread.plainAction: Check the site again at the "Polite" speed, so it asks for pages more slowly.

start-not-root.plainText: This site check started from a page inside your site, not from its home page, so it can't judge the site as a whole.
start-not-root.plainAction: Start the check from your home page, then check the site again.

external-links-off.plainText: This site check was set not to try links to other websites.
external-links-off.plainAction: Check the site again, with "Links to other websites" ticked.

resources-off.plainText: This site check was set not to load images and other files.
resources-off.plainAction: Check the site again, with "Images and other files" ticked.

hreflang-off.plainText: This site check was set not to read the other language versions your pages name, and some of them weren't read.
hreflang-off.plainAction: Tick the setting that reads your other language versions in the check's Advanced settings, then check the site again.

robots-txt-ignored.plainText: This site check was set to ignore your site's rules files for search engines, so it can't say what they put off limits or whether each can be read.
robots-txt-ignored.plainAction: Set the check to follow the rules files again in its Advanced settings, then check the site again.

site-versions-unchecked.plainText: The site's other addresses (with and without www, http and https) couldn't all be tried.
site-versions-unchecked.plainAction: Check the site again to include it.

rule-failed.plainText: Shouting Iguana hit an error of its own while working out this result, so there is nothing to show.
rule-failed.plainAction: Update the results, and if it happens again, treat it as a fault in Shouting Iguana, not in your site.

earlier-version.plainText: This site check was made with an older version of Shouting Iguana, which didn't save what this check compares.
earlier-version.plainAction: Check the site again to include it.

newer-than-analysis.plainText: This check was added to Shouting Iguana after these results were worked out.
newer-than-analysis.plainAction: Update the results to include it.
